newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: Sandinista protest strikes fear into business.
newsitem.headline: Sandinista protest strikes fear into business.

text.p: Growing political instability in the wake of last month's presidential election is sending waves of anxiety through Nicaragua's business community, economists said on Thursday.

The left-wing Sandinista Front's rebellion against alleged fraud in the Oct. 20 presidential election has many business people fearing for the country's economic, as well as political, future, the economists said

The Sandinistas plans to culminate their protest on Friday when the party has called a "day of civic protest" against alleged "massive irregularities" in the vote, apparently won by Arnoldo Aleman of the right-wing Liberal Alliance.

Election officials were to announce the provisional final results of the vote count late on Thursday, threatening to turn Friday's protest into a powder keg if, as expected, they confirm the Sandinista loss.

Sandinista activists have a history of violent protests. The National Police, which had banned public demonstrations in light of post-vote tensions, has not yet said if it will permit the Sandinista protest.

"If there is no political stability there will be no economic take-off. Only the fact that the Sandinista Front has not accepted the results of these elections has caused two major investment projects for Nicaragua to be postponed until January," said Nicaraguan economist Eduardo Montiel, who would not identify the projects.

Montiel, on the morning television talk show Buenos Dias, said the investments would leave Nicaragua for good if the political problems continue. He added his voice to a growing chorus of business leaders and economists concerned about damage the post-election turmoil is doing to the economy.

What was to have been a business celebration, with the pro-free market Aleman defeating former Marxist President Daniel Ortega at the polls, has been clouded by lingering political instability brought on by delays in the vote count.

Eighteen days after the vote, winners still had not been announced, creating political tensions fed by charges of fraud and wild, premature victory celebrations. The preliminary vote count gave Aleman a 49 to 38 percent lead over Ortega, who has refused to concede defeat.
The Nicaraguan Chamber of Commerce has reported a 25 to 30 percent drop in business since the post-vote crisis started.

"The post-electoral tensions have been more damaging than the pre-electoral period," Chamber of Commerce President Alberto Lacayo told reporters. "The march announced by the Sandinistas is a negative factor that affects the normal unfolding of the electoral process."
